That the recommendations contained in the second report of the select standing committee on industrial and international relations presented to the house on May 1st last be concurred in.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT
speechtext:
Notice of this motion
has been given since May 1, and I think it has stood long enough. I am ready to go on with this motion to-day.
The report presented to the house by the committee on industrial and international relations on the first day of May, and printed in the votes and proceedings of May 1, No. 52, is a report based on a resolution adopted by this house on February 14. That resolution, after adoption by the house, was sent to the committee for investigation and report, the committee being instructed to investigate and report on insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity. The house will remember that last year this same resolution was before the committee on industrial and international relations, and last year's report was adopted by the house on June 6th. That report is of importance at the present time.
Before entering into an analysis of last year's report, I should like to say on behalf of the committee of which I am chairman that we have done our best during the last two years to unravel this complicated question and bring in a report that would be favoured by the house. If there is any fault to find with the report I believe that it can be traced to the fact that the resolution which was before the house was not considered seriously enough before being sent on to the committee. I believe the committee has done excellent work. I am not speaking for myself as chairman of the committee, but I believe that we have given to the resolution all the time, care and study that was possible. Lord Disraeli once said that man has been made to adore and obey. I do not know about the adoration so far as this committee's work is concerned, but I do know that the committee has tried to obey the instructions of the house, to investigate and report on a very difficult question, one of the most technical questions that can come before any committee of the house. There is more than one viewpoint to consider when ex*
2772	COMMONS
Industrial Relations-Mr. McIntosh
amining a question of this kind. It needs not only vision to see the problem in hand, but a little sentiment also to warm up to a resolution of that nature, and then it is for the committee to do its best in an executive way to bring in a report that will be satisfactory to the house and to the country.
Hon. members will notice that in the treaty of Peace, in section 1 of part XIII, dealing with labour and the question of universal peace, the statement is made, and I believe it is true, that if we want universal peace in the world it must be based on social justice. If we are to have social justice we must pay attention to some of the fundamentals of labour.
The preamble of this labour section of the treaty of peace first of all deals with a number of important questions affecting labour. It speaks of the injustice and hardship surrounding, for instance, the control of labour; secondly, of insurance against unemployment, sickness, invalidity and old age; thirdly, of the necessary organization and association to bring labour problems before the public; it also deals with the special need for vocational and technical education. These are some of the labour problems that we must face if we are to solve the problems of the labour world and do social justice to all in need in order to bring about national and international peace. They are ideas which concern the justice of labour, and must be carried into effect if humanity is to play its part in solving problems of this kind.
The report that was presented to the house last year was divided into numerous parts. The committee took the stand, in the first place, that unemployment is an important national problem, and a problem that must be faced and solved if we are to solve the problems of the labour world during the next few years. We cannot dodge the issue; we must face it provincially and nationally. Some hon. members may think that a resolution of this kind is not very important, but it is bound to assume more and more importance as the years pass by.
In the second clause of last year's report the committee took a square stand on the question of unemployment insurance; that is, insurance against unemployment based on compulsory contributions by the employer, the employee, and the state. The next clause in that report, which was adopted by the house on June 6th last year, places the responsibility for unemployment insurance upon the different provinces. It was a question that the committee considered to be one of provincial jurisdiction.

The committee next drew attention to the fact that in Canada we have not got the necessary data upon which to base the approximate cost of an unemployment insurance scheme in Canada, and it asked the Labour department at Ottawa to get to work during the ensuing year and do its best to provide that data.
The other clause in the report was to the effect that the committee would like to reinvestigate the question this session. We have spent one or two months on this work.
The resolution this year again deals with insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity. The report presented a few days ago to a large extent covers the same ground as the report of last session, with one or two new features.
The committee, after investigating as far as possible the subject matter of the resolution, took pretty much the same ground as I have mentioned, last year, that' insurance against unemployment should be based on a eompuulsory foundation.	Since the matter is one of provincial jurisdiction, and since all the provinces last year were notified of the report of the committee and replied that	they were not
ready to take any action, the present committee recommended: that the Department of National Health be asked to initiate a comprehensive health program by cooperating with the provincial and municipal health departments; that in the forthcoming census provision be made to register all unemployment and sickness in Canada, and that when that data is secured it should be compiled and published as quickly as possible; that when I he next provincial-federal conference is held, the Dominion government should invite the representatives of organized labour and of organized industry to be present to discuss the subject matter of the report.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the present report to a large extent follows the lines of that presented last year; they have certain points in common. Briefly, both recommend compulsory contributions from the state, the employer and the employee. As the subject matter falls within the competency of the provincial authorities, the committee recommends that action be taken by the legislatures of the respective provinces. The committee recognizes the importance of securing all the data possible on sickness insurance.
This is a very important problem, Mr. Speaker, and the time has now arrived when the report of the committee should be concurred in by the house or rejected. I believe (hat many hon. members may not be cog-

Industrial Relations-Mr. Heaps
nizant of the subject matter of the investigation, 'but I believe there are others who are quite anxious to see something tangible result from it, and the sooner this report is thoroughly debated so the country and parliament may know where we are at, the better it will be for all concerned.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT
speechtext:
With the hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. McIntosh), Mr. Speaker, I realize (he very great importance of the subject matter of this report. I have followed the chairman of the committee with a great deal of interest and the closest atention in the hope that he might give the house a little more enlightenment as to what is really contained in the report.
I am one of those in this house who do not feel satisfied with the recommendations embodied in the report. I have gone into the matter rather carefully, I have attended as many of the meetings as I possibly could, and although I am not a member of the committee I appreciate the many courtesies that were extended to me by its members. They went about their work in the most diligent manner, they examined a great many witnesses, and I had hoped that after the recommendations presented last year, we might have had something more tangible as a result of their labours this session.
There has been, I believe, a great deal of unfair criticism levelled against the work of that committee. With such criticism I have absolutely no sympathy whatsoever. Nevertheless, I do think that constructive criticism -and that is the form I wish to employ on this particular question-is the kind that the chairman of the committee and the whole house will welcome.
The state has a certain responsibility to the man or woman who happens to be out of work. I believe the employer has also a certain amount of responsibility. As recorded in the report last year, it was the intention of that committee that a form of such insurance should be compulsory and be participated in by the state, the employer and the employee. With that suggestion I have no quarrel, because it follows the practice of other countries which have had similar schemes in operation for a number of years.
Last session the house accepted the principle of compulsory unemployment and sickness insurance. We are asked this year to adopt the principle once again. Personally I do not see the necessity of asking the house to endorse the same principle twice. When the committee was asked this year again to consider the question, the intention behind the
resolution was for them to bring forward something more concrete than they submitted last year. In this case I must disagree with what the chairman has had to say. I regard this report as a step backwards, and I shall try to prove this to the house.
Now, the chairman of the committee in bringing this matter before the house, stated that the question was a national problem. With that statement I am in hearty agreement. If it is a national program, then I think it must be dealt with in a national manner, and not in a provincial manner. In section 3 of the report of last year, dated June 1, 1928-and the report was adopted by the house-the following recommendation is contained:
That the evidence of the Justice department makes it clear that the responsibility for such legislation rests on the provincial authorities, it being within their jurisdiction under the provisions of the British North America Act, but that it would be within the power of parliament to contribute, by grant, to such provinces as adopted such legislation, following the precedent set in the matter of technical education, highway construction, and, more recently, the Old Age Pension Act.
Now that was the recommendation of the committee last year and it was unanimously adopted by the house. This year what do the committee recommend? A comparison of the two recommendations will show my hon. friend the chairman of the committee (Mr. McIntosh), and hon. members of the house generally, just why I regard the present report as a backward step. Paragraph 2 of the report this year has the following to say with reference to the question of jurisdiction:
Your committee recognizes that while it is highly desirable that such legislation should be uniform in all the provinces, and while social insurance has a federal aspect, nevertheless, according to the Department of Justice, under our constitution legislative jurisdiction in relation to the establishment of a compulsory system of unemployment insurance as vested exclusively in the provincial legislatures.
And it stops there. Hon. members will here observe the difference between the report of the committee last year and the report submitted this year: last year they stated that the Dominion parliament might, if it so desired, assist in some way in the matter of legislation of this character, just as it has assisted under the Old Age Pensions Act; this year they claim in the report that the matter is entirely one within provincial jurisdiction. Now if we were to depend entirely upon the strict letter of the British North America Act, there are a great many things which this parliament has undertaken which would never have been put into force. The fact is that we have tried to find ways and means of over-

Industrial Relations-Mr. Heaps
coming some obstacles in the British North America Act in order that we might be able to put certain legislation into effect. Let us suppose, Mr. Speaker, that this parliament bad taken, in respect to the question of old age pensions, the attitude which the committee has taken on the question of social insurance: there would never have been any .Old Age Pensions Act on the statutes of this Dominion.
Again, in its report this year, the committee states that the provincial legislatures were not anxious to come within the provisions of such legislation. Let me once more refer to the question of old age pensions. If we had waited until all the provinces had signified their intention to take advantage of that legislation there would be to-day no Old Age Pensions Act on the statute books of Canada. Well, the very same thing applies now to social insurances. In this regard I venture to make this observation. Since last year, and since the beginning of this session, there seems to have been a change of opinion on the part of certain ministers of the crown. A few months ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) described as a vicious principle what he regarded as an encroachment by the federal authorities into the provincial sphere; he said that there should be a clear line of demarcation between the work of the provinces and the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. I am just wondering whether the report submitted by the committee this year does not cany out that view indicated by the Prime Minister in this house some months ago in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. However, I hope I am wrong in that surmise. Personally I hold that the questions of unemployment, sickness and invalidity insurance Should be mainly a Dominion responsibility, and1 I believe that if the government is willing it can find ways and means of overcoming any obstacle in the way of jurisdiction as between the provinces and the Dominion. In this connection I wish to read a paragraph from the platform of the Liberal party-I am sure the government is not going to go 'back on its own platform of 1921.

Well, I regard this as a very good chart, exactly as I am going to regard the Conservative party's platform of 1927 on the same question. Reading from this chart or platform I find at page 9 the following reference to this matter:
That in so far as may be practicable, having regard for Canada's financial position, an adequate system of insurance against unemployment, sickness, dependence in old age and other disability, which would include old age pen-
sions, widows' pensions, and maternity benefits, should be instituted by the federal government in conjunction with the governments of the several provinces; and that on matters pertaining to industrial and social legislation an effort should be made to overcome any question of jurisdiction between the Dominion and the provinces by effective cooperation between the several governments.
I hope I am not asking too much of the government when I suggest to them on this occasion that they put iwto effect their own platform of 1921 just on the eve of the election. And having read that particular plank in the Liberal party's platform, I turn now to the more recent convention held by the Conservative party in the city of Winnipeg. I do not know whether the environment of Winnipeg made them think of social insurance, but if it did I am glad that the Conservative party's convention was held in that city. Let me read just one or two paragraphs from their platform in regard to what they term capital and labour. Beginning with paragraph 9, they say:
So far as is practicable-
Mark you, exactly the same words as used by the Liberal party in 1921. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) asks me whether this is a chart. No doubt they are both charts, but at any rate I am going to ask that legislation be enacted along the lines charted by both parties:
So far as is practicable, to support social legislation designed to conserve human life, health and temperance, to relieve distress during periods of unemployment, sickness and old age.
This is substantially, in effect, the same as the resolution adopted by the Liberal party in 1921. On a previous occasion I expressed ' the opinion that when the house is too unanimous on a question we generally get nowhere. I hope I am not justified in that opinion and I trust that on this occasion, in view of the unanimity of the Liberal and Conservative parties on this question, something in the way of definite legislation will result from the present committee's deliberations.
To the working people of this country this is probably the most important question that has come before the house this year; I do not think I am exaggerating in the slightest degree when I say that in the report submitted this afternoon at least 25 per cent of the people of Canada are vitally interested. Legislation along the lines I have suggested would affect that proportion of the population. Of course, I realize the difficulties in the way of enacting such legislation; but the average man and woman are not very much concerned with difficulties of jurisdiction, as

Industrial Relations-Mr. Neill
between the provinces and the Dominion. We overcame one difficulty in 1926 in connection with old age pensions and there is no reason why we cannot ovecome the same difficulty in relation to legislation of this character. It appears to me that if the house adopts, as it stands, the report of this committee it will be shirking its responsibility, because the whole responsibility will then rest on the provinces; and if we asked the provinces to enact such legislation it would mean that no legislation would be enacted. I cannot imagine that one province would enact a scheme of insurances while neighbouring provinces did not pass similar legislation. I can understand the situation in regard to old age pensions legislation, which is on a basis entirely different from that of a scheme of social insurances. No question of insurance is involved in the old age pension legislation; it is entirely a contribution by the state to aged persons requiring assistance. Therefore in one sense it is not such a great hardship if persons in one province do not obtain old age pensions while persons in another province are given that assistance, but in the case of social insurance in which unemployment, sickness and invalidity are involved, and where there is compulsory contribution to such a scheme by the employees, that is on an entirely different basis. Let us imagine for a moment that in the province of Ontario it was desired to adopt such a scheme; we can understand how difficult it would be for a man living in Ottawa and working in Hull. It would be almost impossible to work out such a scheme unless there was uniform legislation in all the provinces. In order to obtain the uniformity which is necessary there must be some central and responsible body to enact that legislation, and the only responsible and central body is this Dominion parliament.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if possible I would like to help the committee out on this question. According to this motion they now wish to put the whole responsibility on the provinces, but in this country we cannot have nine different schemes of social insurance; I would much prefer one scheme enacted by the federal parliament, and I believe there is a way out of the difficulty. It is a debatable question whether or not this parliament has sufficient jurisdiction in this matter, but assuming we have not that jurisdiction we can do in this matter just as we did in connection with the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. Under that act the powers vested in some of the provinces have been handed over by them to the Dominion parliament,
and now this parliament has the full right to legislate with regard to industrial disputes in those provinces, under t'he provisions ol the act to which I have just referred.
Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I would like to see this report referred back to the committee. I know that by so doing at this stage of the session it will mean that the report is dead so far as this year is concerned, but I will take full responsibility for such action. I would much prefer to have this report killed than to have this house adopt a report which means practically nothing to the vast majority of the working people in this country. I think if the report went back and the committee considered the suggestion I now make, that the provincial authorities vest in the Dominion authority the right to legislate in connection with unemployment, sickness and invalidity insurance, we would be taking a step forward. Even in this report it is claimed that this should be a matter for federal legislation, in order that the legislation might be uniform, and if this is ithe case I think we should at least try to bring into being such uniform legislation by a federal enactment.
Therefore I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill):
That the said report of the select standing committee on industrial and international relations be not now concurred in hut that it be referred back to the select standing committee on industrial and international relations with instructions that they have power to amend the same by adding thereto a clause recommending that all the provinces of the Dominion be requested to pass legislation under which the jurisdiction in relation to legislation providing for unemployment, sickness and invalidity insurance based on compulsory contribution and which is now claimed to be within or subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces be vested in the Dominion government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself in a rather ambiguous position with regard to this matter; I am seconding a resolution moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) asking to amend the report of a committee of which I was a member, and in whose report I acquiesced. However, I am prepared to take the full responsibility for my action; I could not think of a better solution of the problem before us, and. somewhat shamefacedly I am compelled to say to my hon. friend from North Winnipeg, in the words of Kipling, "You're a better man than I am, Gunga Din." I only hope this condition will not become habitual.
The report of the committee deals with the question of unemployment in three sections; first it endorses the principle which we en-
2776	COMMONS
Industrial Relations-Mr. Neill
dorsed last year and then it says that the provinces, on being consulted, apparently were not prepared for immediate action. The provinces were very wishy-washy in their answers; some of them merely acknowledged receipt of the letter, and no province exhibited' the slightest interest in the matter. The third and the only active suggestion contained in this report is that in the forthcoming census provision should be made for the securing of the fullest possible data with regard to the extent of unemployment and sickness, and that this information should be compiled and published as soon as possible. I must confess that when we drew up that report I felt this to be quite inadequate, because the census will not be taken for another two years, and two or three^ years more will elapse before that information is compiled, tabulated and published, so it will be practically useless.
If I remember correctly, in the report of this committee last year it was suggested that the Labour department should take steps to ascertain by practical methods, from month to month, the extent of unemployment in Canada. Some of the officials of that department appeared before the committee this year and stated that this was practically impossible. I do not think it is impossible, and I believe a better attempt could and should have been made to obtain that information. The officials did not say it was absolutely impossible; they said it would involve enormous expense, but I do not agree with that contention either.
The hon. member for North Winnipeg has stated that the adoption of this amendment would mean the abandonment of any report from this committee this year. Seeing the nature of the report I think no great hardship will result if the matter is held over for another year, because the census will not be held for two years, and that is the only practical suggestion contained in the report. This amendment does contain a practical, concrete suggestion, and it does seem to clear the air of this continual miasma which we meet at every turn, as to the respective jurisdiction of the Dominion and of the provinces. We have been travelling around and around that question for the last two years in this committee; we have had reports and opinions from the legal officers and so on, 'but we do not seem to go ahead. As the hon. member stated, a precedent exists for this action; a similar policy was adopted when the provinces waived their rights under the Industrial Disputes Act, turning them over to the Dominion. That gave the Dominion full jurisdiction; that appears to have worked well and I see no reason why it should not work well in this case also.

speechtext: Does my hon. friend think the provinces have the right to do that without. an amendment to the British North America Act?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT
speechtext: Yes, because whatever divergence of opinion there may be as to the rights of the provinces, we must accept the fact that they have some rights, and if the provinces pass legislation turning over these rights, whatever they may be, to the Dominion, certainly I think that would be constitutional.

speechtext:
Does not
my hon. friend think it would be more intelligent to proceed in this way: Have the federal parliament pass the legislation which is desired and make it operative only after concurrent legislation has been passed by the respective provinces?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT
speechtext: No, that principle was adopted in the Old Age Pension Act and it was made permissive to each province. The general scheme of unemployment, owing to its very nature, could not be made provincially permissive; it would have to be universal, and for that reason we would desire to have it handled by the one federal authority.

That the said report of the select standing committee on industrial and international relations be not now concurred in but that it be referred back to the select standing committee on industrial and international relations with instructions that they have power to amend the same by adding thereto a clause recommending that all the provinces of the Dominion be requested to pass legislation under which the jurisdiction in relation to legislation providing for unemployment, sickness and invalidity insurance. based on compulsory contribution and which is now claimed to be within or subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, be vested in the Dominion government.
Does the hon. gentleman suggest that, when specific jurisdiction is vested under the constitution in the provinces, the provinces by any conceivable legislation could revest that jurisdiction in the Dominion parliament? It seems to me to be the most extraordinary suggestion I have heard for some time.

speechtext: Will the hon. minister explain how the authority was given under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: That is quite different. The hon. member proposes in his amendment that it would of necessity be a compulsory contribution. A compulsory contribution by employers and by employees, as has been said in the house, is undoubtedly a matter of civil rights as it affects the civil rights of both the employers and the employees, and it comes clearly and exclusively within the scope of the matters assigned to the provinces for legislation under the British North America Act.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT
speechtext: Are there ho civil rights under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT
speechtext: There was no compulsion placed upon anyone. That act had to be changed in order to make it constitutional, as my hon. friend knows. That act was declared unconstitutional by the Privy Council and we had to change it and limit it to federal matters which came within the powers of this federal legislature. We offered the machinery of the Labour department and of this enactment to the provinces who might ask this parliament to put that machinery at their disposal in the case of industrial disputes.

speechtext: Did not the provinces surrender certain rights which they claimed to be provincial?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT
speechtext: They passed enabling legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN COMMITTEE'S REPORT
speechtext:
I am quite sure that the provinces would never agree to this parliament imposing contributions and taxation on their citizens in matters which were undoubtedly provincial; they would not agree to that, and even if they did agree I do not think they would have the right to do so. The provinces have the right to delegate certain powers to municipalities, to commissions and to bodies which are of their own creation, and those bodies have the right to pass regulations and by-laws, but the provinces under the provisions of the British North America Act cannot delegate those powers to the federal parliament. That act is a charter- it is not a chart as explained by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) a few minutes ago-of the provinces and a charter of the Dominion, and neither one has the right to change it. If my hon. friend will not accept my views in this matter perhaps he will accept the views of the Privy Council. I have here the words of Lord Watson, given in a case reported in Lefroy's Canada's Federal System, in which he said:
The Dominion cannot give jurisdiction, or leave jurisdiction, with the province. The provincial parliament cannot give legislative jurisdiction to the Dominion parliament. If they have it, either one or the other of them, they have it by virtue of the act of 1867. I think we must get rid of the idea that either one or the other can enlarge the jurisdiction of the other or surrender jurisdiction.
To these remarks Lord Davey added, "or curtail."

speechtext: Have you the reference from which you are quoting?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
This is in the course of the argument in Canadian Pacific R. W. Co. versus Bonsecours, (1899) A.C. 367.
Sir John Thompson, when Minister of Justice in 1889-the house will find his words on page 218 of the same book-said that he had to express his dissent from the view:
-that the interpretation of the British North America Act can in any way he affected by subsequent legislation by parliament, or the legislatures, or by any action of the government. No legislative body can. by legislation, increase or diminish the authority conferred upon it by the constitution, nor can any expression of opinion or course of legislative action by either afford any conclusive or even satisfactory guide to its interpretation.
No person in Canada can be hound by acquiescence in unconstitutional legislation on the on the part of governments, even if such acquiescence has occurred.
It is an elementary principle that governments, no more than individuals, can do indirectly what they cannot do directly. In that regard I will read two leading propositions of Lefroy in his book entitled Canada's Federal System. They are propositions Nos. 17 and 18, as follows:
17. The parliament of Canada cannot under colour of general legislation deal with what

But if one goes beyond the wording of any resolution or report of a committee, one must come to the conclusion that this is another exemplification of what is coming to us from year to year as a growing truth, that we have outgrown the literal bounds of the written constitution under which we live. There is not the slightest doubt that when this constitution was framed neither the upholders of legislative union nor the defenders of provincial rights ever anticipated the immense importance which labour problems would assume. They never anticipated that this question of social insurance, whether applying to unemployment, to sickness, or to any other form of social suffering, would be of such importance that it is now one of the national problems with which we have to deal.
If we take this factor as existing to-day in this year of our Lord, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-nine, a factor which is growing fast upon us, which will be more important next year and the year following than it is now, we cannot solve the problem by looking into this or that clause, or word, or semicolon of the charter under which we are governed. We must find some means to adjust those problems, and we must devise a way to come to an agreement with the various provinces wherever provincial jurisdiction is an obstacle to the exercise of national jurisdiction by the federal parliament. It seems to me that it is an imperative duty upon us.
To claim that because civil rights and property are under provincial jurisdiction this parliament is debarred, legally and constitutionally, from the accomplishment of its duty to the people of Canada at large in regard to those great social problems-I cannot agree to that. Whether or not we could by some means legislate upon this question of social insurance without an amendment to the constitution I do not know. I do not pretend to the legal knowledge and experience that may be necessary to settle that first point. But I know this, that on many other questions of state and legislation, experience has proven that the general jurisdiction exercised by the parliament of Canada for the good of Canada at large, or according to the usual phraseology " for the general advantage of Canada," has in many instances overcome the objection of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. May I quote one or two examples? With regard to the law of bankruptcy, it was questioned for many years in the province of Quebec whether this parliament had the right or the jurisdiction to legislate upon that matter, because once a law of bankruptcy
was enacted by this parliament it would of necessity amend, directly or indirectly, the civil code with regard to the application of many articles of that code, promissory notes, interest, and so forth.

Now, with regard to railways, I remember a famous case in the province of Quebec a case which was pleaded by one of the most eminent lawyers of that province, the late Sir Lomer Gouin, who became premier of Quebec and afterwards Minister of Justice in this government. It was a case in which the sole issue was a conflict between the right exercised by the individual, under a certain article of the civil code, to enjoy his property as against damages sustained through the acts, whether culpable or not, of another party, and, on the other hand, the jurisdiction granted by this parliament to the railway company to operate its railways as a common conveyance, whatever might be the consequences to individuals. The question of fact was not disputed; it was admitted that the railway company had done all it could to ensure the preservation of private properties along the roads traversed by its railways. Fire was set to the individual's building by the engine of one of the company's trains and that individual sued the company. He pleaded that article of the civil code under which he was entitled to enjoy his property and under w'hich he claimed that the railway company was responsible for all its acts. But the Privy Council decided that, parliament having granted, for the general advantage of Canada, the power to that company to run its trains throughout Canada, the right of the individual under the civil code must yield to the right of the company under that federal legislation. I cite this not as a legal point touching the matter now under discussion, but simply by way of illustration of the problems that arise day by day, placing us in the position of having to choose between the discharge of our duty to the people of Canada at large, and a scrupulous respect for the letter of the constitution

I am second to none in my respect for the basic principles of the constitution. But, I repeat, we must go ahead. This country must face its duties and the problems that arise from year to year. We cannot remain shackled by the strict letter of a constitution which was written some sixty years ago and which no longer corresponds to all the needs of the people. It is from that point of view particularly, leaving aside the wording either of the committee's report or of the proposed amendment, that I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) that this matter should be referred back to the' committee for more careful consideration at another session; because if we go on at this rate, many problems that ought to be seriously studied and ultimately solved by this parliament or by the various legislatures of the country will remain unsolved, or will be delayed to the detriment of all the provinces and of the whole population at large.
We cannot divide this country into nine compartments labelled Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and so on, for the simple reason that each compartment or province has its raison d'etre. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has said, this is a confederacy and ought to remain a confederacy. But Canada is also a nation; it is one country and ought to be broad enough, with a constitution flexible enough, to meet the needs of all classes of the population irrespective of province, race or any other consideration. Now these labour problems, these social insurance problems, are essentially national questions. If you wait for the nine legislatures of Canada all to deal with the situation, you will wait a long time. The reason is obvious: the labour problem may be a rural problem in one province; it may be an industrial problem in another province; or it may affect a large proportion of the population in one province and a small proportion of the population in another. We have to admit, human nature being what it is. that governments and legislatures are mainly concerned with those problems that are sufficiently acute to force themselves upon public opinion in the respective provinces. And if this social question is not of , immediate concern to the government of one or another of the nine provinces, that government will take no stock in it inasmuch as the question will have no bearing upon the next provincial election. The result is that that particular province will stand as an obstacle to the action of the Dominion or of the other provinces that happen to be more concerned in the matter. I submit, therefore, that if we have to wait until the [Mr. Bourassa.)
nine provinces are of one accord on every single aspect of this question we shall wait a long time; and in that event we shall remain far in the rear of all those countries which, having to face these social problems, have at least taken some action-action which, while ,not always leading to perfection, has at any rate brought such countries nearer a solution of their difficulties.
I do not think we should shelter ourselves for any length of time under the protection of constitutional rights, thus refraining from dealing with these problems. I must confess, as a member of the committee, that I was not as faithful and constant an attendant at its meetings as 1 should have been had I not been otherwise busily engaged. I may say, however, that I have followed its proceedings with sufficient care, and have read sufficiently in various publications appearing not only in this countiy and the United States but in Europe as well, to realize that we are far behind most other countries in dealing with social problems; and largely as a result of this situation which has presented itself to-day, as it has done on many other occasions in relation to social and other problems, whenever the question has arisen as to the respective jurisdiction of the provinces and of the federal government, we find ourselves taking the attitude that we cannot deal with the matter for the reason that it affects provincial rights. Some province will say. " We will not deal with it because, irrespective of what the people of the other provinces may feel, our people are not interested in the question." Another province will say, " Let the federal government deal with the situation."

In my view, this is a constitutional question. Bourinot, in defining the powers of the Speaker, says at page 180: [Mr Adshead.l
He will not give a decision upon a constitutional question, nor decide a question of law, though the same be raised on a point of order or privilege.
I have no doubt that this question is constitutional; that is to say, it involves a change in connection with the respective powers of the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures. To make such a change in the constitution requires a joint address of both houses of parliament to the Imperial parliament.
A similar question arose some years ago, in 1903, when I was a young member of the House of Commons. After the census of 1901, the province of Prince Edward Island lost two members, and when the new redistribution based on the census was being put through the house, a motion was made in the House of Commons by Mr. Hackett, one of the members from Prince Edward Island, seconded by the hon. member for Lincoln, Ontario, Mr. Lancaster, to the effect that in spite of the census the representation of Prince Edward Island should be six members instead of four. Thereupon the Prime Minister of the day said:
I submit that this amendment is out of order, because it is contrary to the constitution.. The constitution* provides for representation by population between the provinces. The very question raised in this amendment has been submitted to the supreme court, Which has decided that the province of Prince Edward Island and all the other provinces are entitled to the number of members which are mentioned in this bill. The British North AmeVica Act provides that the representation of the other provinces shall be based upon the unit fixed by the representation of Quebec, and this amendment would violate that provision of the British North America Act.
Just as this amendment violates one of the provisions of the British North America Act, as was pointed out by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). The Speaker of that day gave this ruling:
The question which has been raised in regard to the amendment is a very difficult one, and I am very sorry that I have not had more time at my disposal to give it the fullest consideration. It would appear, as has been stated before the house, that this parliament has not the necessary legislative authority to grant Prince Edward Island the number of members asked for by this amendment and the supreme court, having been consulted upon the matter, declared that the British North America Act does not give to the province the right to have more than four members.
He goes on:
According to rule 37 of the House of Commons, the Speaker has the right to declare out of order any motion contrary to the rules and privileges of parliament. I see that there is a

Industrial Relations-Mr. Bennett
very serious doubt, whether under our rules of procedure the Speaker has the right on his own authority to interfere and declare irregular and out of order a motion of this kind. May, at page 331, says:
"But doubtful cases may arise, upon which the rules of the house are indistinct or obsolete, or do not apply strictly to the point at issue; when the Speaker, being left without specific directions, refers the matter to the judgment of the house."
I am of the opinion, under the circumstances, that, on account of the serious doubt which may arise as to the irregularity of the motion made by the hon. member for West Prince, I should leave it to the house to determine whether this motion is irregular or not, or whether it should be accepted or not.
In my own mind, I have no doubt as to the unconstitutionality of the amendment if it were carried, but Bourinot says that the Speaker cannot decide on constitutional questions. and therefore I think the best way is for the house to pronounce on the amendment now that the members have been called in.

While in the west
during the last recess, I was approached by some veterans of the South African war. They pointed out to me that almost all our other legislation dealing with returned men had been so amended as to give to veterans of the South African war practically the same terms, in every respect, as were conceded to veterans of the Great war. In the matter of pensions, in the matter of hospitalization, in practically every measure introduced in relation to the reestablishment of returned soldiers of the last war, the South African veterans, it was stated, had been placed on a parity with their brothers. But it was pointed out to me that in this one particular there was an exception, and it was urged upon me with a good deal of force and, I may say, quite convincingly by a man with whom I am very well acquainted, that this entailed a real hardship. A South African veteran who had lost his leg as the result of services at that time had volunteered for service in the expeditionary force in the Great war but naturally was not accepted on account of his physical condition. He has a pension with which, in addition to what he can earn, he supports himself, an invalid and widowed mother and one or two helpless members of the family. Not long ago he made an attempt to obtain insurance under this act which would enable his mother and other dependents to carry on in case of his death. He made his application in good faith, enclosing the amount required as a premium 78594-178
for a S3,000 policy, but of course he was informed that this act did not include South African veterans but only veterans of the Great war. He spoke to me on the subject and I must say he was very convincing, so much so that at least I saw the justice of his contention, particularly as this would affect comparatively few men. So I told him that as far as I could see the matter was fair and that I would bring it to the attention of the minister having charge of the act and all the members of the cabinet, who are anxious to see justice done to all returned soldiers so far as that is possible.
I would like to know from the minister if he would consider the extension of the benefits of this insurance act to that comparatively small handful of veterans who remain from the South African war, who as I said before have been placed on a parity with other veterans in everj'thing except this matter. If they could come in under this act they would come under exactly the same terms, regulations and laws under which the veterans of the Great war now carry on, and I would be very glad if this question could be considered. I do not feel that it would involve a great deal of money; there are not very many of these men left, and those men who were crippled in the South African war and who have lived up to the present time obviously were not those who were in immediate danger of death.
Hon. iR. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition): Before the minister replies I might state that representations were made to me by a substantial number of South African returned men on this particular question, and I had intended to bring up the matter. By way of preface to the remarks I am going to make I wish to read something from the act. Section 4 of chapter 90 of the Revised Statutes of Canada is as follows:
The duties and powers of the minister administering the Department of Health shall extend to and include all matters and questions relating to the promotion or preservation of the health of the people of Canada over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction, and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, particularly the following matters and subjects:

If we could advance the life expectancy in Canada by two years, with our 9,000,000 people and figuring the increase in wealth at $100 per year per capita, we would add- to the wealth of the country the huge sum of $1,800,000,000. The house knows that serum was discovered by injecting the poisons of diphtheria into a horse and the anti-toxin was formed in its blood; after a sufficient quantity had formed it was bled and the serum was purified and kept in a ready condition to be administered to children or anyone who got the disease. In connection with typhoid fever it was discovered that by sterilizing the bacillus typhus and injecting it into a human being an anti-toxin could be obtained which would practically prevent the disease. That disease is practically extinct to-day. I looked up the records of twenty-four of the largest cities in the United States and I found that the death rate had fallen from 58 per 100,000 down to 8. This is a disease which could be wiped out with proper sanitation and a proper water supply. Many scientists predict that by 1930 diphtheria will be practically a disease of the past. By immunizing children who are susceptible to this disease they feel that it will be practically eliminated in four or five years.
Let us consider the venereal diseases for a moment, and in this connection I would like to quote from a report issued by Justice Hod-gins in 1917. He said:
Speaking generally -the evil is so great and so underspread that nothing would he gained, but rather the reverse by attempting at once too drastic action.
The statistics available at that time show that of the admissions to the Toronto General Hospital in the first three months of that year 12 per cent showed a positive Wasserman reaction; 25 per cent of the male patients at the Toronto hospital for the insane, had syphilis; and 26 per cent of the inmates of the Montreal general hospital were in the same condition. The percentage with refer-

ence to the admissions to the general hospital to-day has dropped to five, while in the case of the admissions to the Sick Children's hospital it is down to less than one per cent. That shows the result of the intensive campaign which has been carried on during the last ten years.
It might be interesting to know, as regards typhoid fever, that prior to and during the South African war, about 85 per cent of war casualities were from disease, principally typhoid fever. In the last war those figures were just about reversed, and it was estimated that from 5 to 10 per cent of the war casualities were from disease and the balance from wounds.
Let us consider for a moment the way in which life expectancy has been increased in other countries. I have under my hand the London Life table, from 1841 to 1922, and the expectancy of life according to that table has increased in males from 34-6 years to 53-8 years, and in females from 38-3 to 59-1 years. This has been brought about largely by preventive measures. If you compute the value of human life even in dollars and cents according to the large increase which has taken place in the expectancy of life, you will see what it is possible to accomplish in this country.
There is another side of the question that I should like to draw to the attention of the committee for a moment, and I should be glad if the Prime Minister would be good enough to take cognizance of the figures I am going to give. Based on the investigation of Professors Winslow and Fisher of Yale university, who with Mr. Doublin' of the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, made in connection with the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, a complete survey of the health of the United States in regard to the iprevention of accidents, sickness and death, and applying the same statistics to Canada-and I think this would be reasonable-we find that the wastage is simply enormous, unbelievable, as I shall show in a moment. These investigations showed that there was a yearly death rate in Canada of 96,000 to 100,000, forty per cent of which was claimed to be preventable. Forty per cent of 96,000 is equivalent to a waste of 38,000 deaths per annum. If you place a valuation of, say $2,500 per annum per life, we have the enormous wastage of $96,000,000. Clitting this in half to make allowance for children, we have a total economic wastage of preventable or postponable deaths of $48,000,000. This applies to preventable deaths alone.

Applying the same principle to illness, we find that two per cent of the population are continuously ill. This means that 180,000 people are continuously ill; of these 30 per cent or 54,000 are adult males and 30 per cent, or 54,000 adult females. The ratio of employment of women to that of men is as 6 is to 20, so we get a total wastage in this way of 16,200 females and 54,000 males, or a total loss of 70,200 people continuously. Allowing 300 working days to the year, we have a total wastage of 21,060,000 days, 50 per cent of which is preventable, or in other words 10,530,000 days. If we take this at a wastage of say $3 per day from each of these workers, we have a further wastage of $31,590,000 from preventable illness. If we could just save that and apply the saving to reducing our national debt, I wonder how soon we could relieve our citizens of the burden of taxation.
But that is not all. They-also found there was an inefficiency due to advanced impairment to health of some 10 to 24 per cent of the working population, while those suffering from minor illnesses range from 18 to 40 per cent. Let us take a fair average of 20 per cent. There are in Canada 3,510,000 wage earners at an average of $750 per annum, giving a total earning capacity of $2,632,500,000. On the above basis 20 per cent of these are inefficient to an extent of 25 per cent inefficiency, or a wastage of $131,625,000. I sometimes think we get into the habit of rolling millions off our tongues so easily that we lose the significance of these figures.
We have invested in hospitals $120,000,000, in sanitoria $50,000,000 and in asylums, $7,500,000, or a 'total of $177,500,000. The cost of upkeep of these institutions is $50,000,000 a year. Of the patients treated in these institutions 40 per cent are suffering from diseases that are preventable.
Adding all these totals, without wearying the house with the figures-and I have cut them in half-we get a total wastage from preventable death, illness, accident and dis-sease, of about $126,530,000 per annum. I should like to direct this to the attention of the house and the committee for the consideration of the Department of Health. This opens up a possible field for active work in this country. How is this wastage to be prevented? It can be prevented in two ways which are outlined in the act which brought this department into existence, first by coordinating all the health efforts of the country, provincial, Dominion and those connected with the insurance companies, so as to reduce the death rate and the preventable illness and

accidents to the lowest possible minimum; second by increasing scientific research. It i? almost inconceivable that the government would stay in power for so many years, with a Department of Health going on year after year, and never creating a department of scientific research. Scientific research is the very basis, the lifeblood of any country. For instance, the work of Pasteur in France in connection with wines, silkworms and anthrax in sheep, brought such a saving to that country that Professor Huxley said that the saving from those three discoveries made by one man would have paid off the Franco-Prussian war debt. I was reading only yesterday the life of Mark Carlton, who turned the state of Kansas into a great wheat-growing country. Away back in the nineties when they struck the wheat rust there, he took his microscope and examined the soil and the grain and travelled all over the world. Finally in Siberia he got a wheat that he brought back and started to grow in the United States, and not many years after that the United States was producing between seven and eight hundred million bushels of wheat a year. He practically put the state of Kansas on the map as a wheat-growing state.
One of the greatest tales of modern times I think is connected with the work of Doctor Gorges, the man who eliminated yellow fever. He got the idea, simply as a general practitioner, that the mosquito was responsible for transmitting yellow fever. Being a man of keen observation he noticed that the higher he went up into the mountains the fewer cases of yellow fever there were, until finally he reached an elevation where a particular kind of mosquito disappeared.	The fever
disappeared also. He came	back and
started his experiments. Some people were of the opinion that the yellow fever was due to insanitary conditions. They cleaned up the insanitary conditions, but the yellow fever prevailed just the same. Still working on his theory that the mosquito was responsible, he built some rooms and covered them with fine netting so that the mosquitoes could not get' in, and he lived there. He took the clothes from the beds of people who had died of yellow fever and slept on them; he put on their clothes, and still he came out untouched by the disease. Then he took some mosquitoes and let them bite him, and in a few days he discovered that he had yellow fever. But working on that hypothesis, a remedy was found, and millions of people have been freed from that disease, and almost half a continent has been reclaimed. As was stated here the other night, the Panama canal could never have been built had this discovery not been made.
What, for instance, would a cure for cancer be worth to this country? I have just read that the death rate from cancer is increasing by leaps and bounds. This country cannot have too many men working in the unknown. The more men we have engaged in original research, the more likely we are to make discoveries of great benefit to humanity. It is only by delving into the unknown and making discoveries such as Doctor Banting made that you will achieve something that will prolong human life and make the human race happier. What, for example, has Doctor Banting's discovery been worth? Take the insurance companies. Every life thait is prolonged means just that much found money for the insurance companies, and expressed in terms of dollars and cents it would no doubt run into billions of dollars in a short time.
I might go on and speak of the discovery of the use of liver extract in curing pernicious anaemia. That was discovered by Doctors Minott and Lea. All these discoveries have helped to prolong human life and have meant greater happiness and greater prosperity for mankind. That is a work that I think this department has been very lax in since it has been organized. I urged upon the minister, when he brought this department into existence, to have research work of this kind started at once, and I got his promise; but shortly after the Liberal government went out of power, and nothing along that line has been done since. If you want expressed in concrete form the results of scientific investigations, I would refer you to the evidence taken by a committee of this house some years ago on scientific and industrial research. We find that one discovery in the Mellon institute, on behalf of a baking firm in the United States, has saved them $500,000 a year. The Eastman Kodak Company has been spending millions ekery year on research, and they have got the business of the world. It is the same with the Dupont Powder and Paint Company. That firm stands in a place by itself to-day. I think the future of this young country with all its vast natural resources is absolutely bound up with and dependent upon industrial and scientific research. I appeal to the Minister of National Health and to the Prime Minister to-night to do something to give this young country a chance with her competitors throughout the world. We have the men, we have the natural resources, we have the opportunity. All we lack is courage on the part of the government to establish in the city of Ottawa a laboratory that will give our young men of ideas a chance to come here and engage in this all-important research work under able direction.

The point I want to bring home is that there is no department of government in this or any other country that offers such opportunities for the creation of wealth, for the saving of waste, for bettering the welfare and increasing the happiness of our people than the Department of Health. speechtext:
It is rather a strange thing that the moment a member speaks on either one of two subjects this house immediately empties itself. Those two subjects are bad whiskey and good health. Either of these subjects just melts the house away. Either will stop a riot and dispense a crowd anywhere. It is unfortunate, but it is so.
We hear a good deal about what is being done in the matter of public health in this country. We have a national Department of Health which was established in 1919. In that year this national institution first saw the light of day; it had an easy birth and the circumstances surrounding its arrival were auspicious. But under the guidance of this government, and with the kindly nutrition handed out to it by the present administration, we find that the poor baby to-day is the same weight and size, and has all the peculiar features which characterized it, as on the day of its birth. In other words, in relation to the Department of Health, the government has stood still for ten years; and what is more, it will stand still for twenty years longer unless someone comes along and wakes it up.
Is it not strange that we should have a Department of Health costing between $900,000 and $1,000,000 a year for the purpose of safeguarding the health of the people, while this government should be spending more than one half-two thirds-of that money on the heads of the department and in administration? Out of this $900,000 per annum spent by the government in the last ten years we find, in 1926, $427,000; in 1927, $393,000; in 1928, $472,000, expended on matters which by no stretch of the imagination can be regarded as conducing to public health. Most of the money comprises grants to the institution.

The government are not spending the money in the way parliament intends that it should be spent; the amount spent on public health as such is absolutely inadequate to accomplish any results. It might as well be wasted. Look at the national budgets of other countries and you will find that in these places, in order to secure anything like a proper standard of public health, it requires an expenditure of $2.50 per capita. But what are we doing in Canada? Instead of spending anything like a reasonable proportion on public health our per capita expenditure amounts to 74 cents. And if we take all the money spent by the Dominion, by the provinces and by the municipalities together, we find that it comes to the magnificent sum of 374 cents per head of population. We are spending in Canada 374 cents per head to accomplish what other countries are spending $2.50 to do. Can we ever dream of having anything like sound national health when such a parsimonious effort is put forth to that end?
It is commonly said that the Dominion government have no authority to act in the matter of public health in Canada. Medical men who have looked into the constitution know that this is not correct. In 1867 when the British North America Act was passed there was no such thing as public health in the sense that we use that term to-day. The only reference to public health was the matter of quarantine, and under section 91 of the act this was assigned to the Dominion government. We know also that matters which are not specifically assigned to any province come, under the British North America Act, within the domain of the Dominion government. Health officers and students in Canada came to the conclusion some time ago that under the constitution matters of public health should rest with the Dominion. We say, therefore, that the government have not been spending the money granted by parliament in the way that it should be spent. Under the act of 1919 it was provided that the government of the Dominion might publish literature, might disseminate propaganda, and might undertake to educate the people of the country in matters appertaining to public health. Well, they have done so, because we have here a magnificent sheet known as an abstract of current public health literature, and blazoned at the head of it is the intimation that it is issued by this government. But what has it to say with reference to public health? We find that, it contains extracts from the Journal of Medical Health of the United States. It tells us how to tackle

the plague in India, how to grapple with cholera in South Africa, and so on. But there is not a word as to what should be done in Canada. It reminds me of a trip I made some fifteen years ago on the Mississippi. Someone pointed out to me one of the old fashioned boats which had plied on the river long years ago-and what did I find? There was so much space taken up by the whistle that there was no room left for the passengers, and in the front of the boat there was a magnificent leather cushioned chair for the captain. Well, we have a chair for the captain to repose in-a captain who draws $15,000 a year but has not been worth ten cents in the ten years he has been guilding the ship in this department.
I want to pay tribute to a gentleman whom we all respect in this house, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Anderson), who gave us an excellent discourse the other evening in which he pointed out what could be accomplished in the way of scientific research. We have also heard a splendid address tonight from my hon. friend (Mr. McGibbon). I am not going to enter into the phase of the subject with which these hon. gentlemen dealt, but I want to say that the Department of National Health is condemned by every man in Canada who has ever read three lines about public health. If you want to find out what is being done in this direction you have only to take up the last journal published by those in this country who are studying the question, and every line is a condemnation of what is being done by the government. It is pointed out that if the government were alive to the situation it would move forward and do things that are being done in other countries. Why is it that France, England and the United States, acting as a federal unit, have all moved forward along really progressive lines? The United States government has divided the country into sections and over every section there ia a full time health officer paid by the federal government.

This is one of the things we ask for. This Dominion should foe divided into health sections, over every one of which should be placed a full time officer paid partly _ by this government, partly by the province and partly foy the municipality. This is one of the things which the public health people of the Dominion are asking the government to do and it is one of the things that are absolutely necessary if we hope to obtain satisfactory results. If the minister wishes to know what can really be accomplished let him
read what has been done in the province of Quebec, which has been divided in the manner I have stated. There full time men are devoting their whole time and all their energies to the work of caring for the public health. See what they have done in relation to infantile mortality and in the matter of saving the lives of women in maternal trouble. See what has been done in grappling with epidemics; it is a credit to the province. They lead the way in this regard. And we have done the same in Ontario. For fifteen years I served as a member of the provincial board of Ontario and I have travelled throughout the province, so that I think I have the right to stand here and say that I speak with some authority on this question. Fifteen years ago in Ontario fifty persons out of every one hundred thousand of the population died of typhoid. The provincial government then grappled with the question and instituted a thorough investigation. We investigated the water supply of the province and looked into the situation from every angle. The result is that we have reduced the death rate in the province, from this particular cause, from 50 to 3.5 per hundred thousand. Such facts as these are pointed out to the government; and to find them, in the face of all this, sitting dumb and motionless is to me a marvel. The people will hold them responsible and get behind those who have progressive ideas with an insistent demand that we advance.
The last issue of the Canadian Public Health Journal, word foy word, line by line, page by page, makes this demand of the government; yet we see the government of Canada hanging on away at the tail end of the hunt, the people a great distance ahead of them. The medical men of the country are miles ahead of the department. We find hon. genltlemen sitting quietly foy, doing nothing but smoking fifty-cent cigars and drawing $15,000 a year. As an immediate steip in the direction of progress we demand that the government make a move in the apointment of a council of epidemiologists. Does the minister mean to tell this committee that if we had a council such as this, a few men who studied nothing but epidemics in Canada, who could move from one section of the country to another whenever there was an outbreak of any epidemic, very satisfactory results would not ensue? Two years ago there was a typhoid epidemic in Montreal when five hundred people were carried to the grave, while some five thousand were down in the hospitals. This cost between two and three millions. I have no hesitation in saying that if we had had in the Dominion at that

As soon as people began to lose a few dollars the cry went up (hat something should be done. In these two particulars we charge the government with dereliction of duty. They have no conception of the task that confronts them ; they do not understand the question with which they are supposed to cope. If you were to engage a few men who really appreciated the value of such measures as I have mentioned, you would see a progressive move made in the matter of public health in Canada. Let me quote something to show what is being done in England in regard to whole time officers. We read that the full time plan is in operation in England, where 351 out of some 1,200 part time officers have been replaced by full time officials in combined areas. In the United States also, since 1911, over 400 county health officers have been appointed on full time. In New York state half the cost is borne by the state. This gives you an idea of what is taking place throughout the civilized world wherever the authorities are alive to the importance of public health, wherever they place a proper value on human life, wherever they have an adequate conception as to what public health implies. In these countries public health work is divided into two great sections-one, the prevention of disease, and the other the combating of epidemics. In this regard disease and epidemics are fought pretty much as an up to date fire brigade tackles any conflagration. What should we think if we went into a large city and saw a great fire being attacked by volunteer firemen, while someone was paid a salary of *15,000 to look on at the show, occasionally to ring a bell, and once in a while to blow a whistle?
I make the charge that Canada, in the field of public health, is more backward than any other country on the face of the earth; the government are silent, they are dead. I do not hesitate to say that. There should be more activity in the department. In 1919 a council of health was created, and they come together every year, bringing scientific minds to bear upon the health problems that confront the 
country. Their conclusions they pass on to the Minister of National Health (Mr. King Kootenay). I say, the people of Canada demand that we have some genuine national health work done by this government, and done before another year goes by. Now, I will not detain the house longer-

I refer to the quarantine service, the medical inspection of immigrants and the treatment of sick mariners. These were the services which our constitution laid down as coming wii'thiin. tihe purview of the Dominion government. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), speaking to-day on another question, made that very plain. But we do not need to emphasize it, because if we take the act that was passed in 1919 we find that the govern-

ment of that day realized the extent to which they should go in establishing a department of health. In the act there are two clauses- it was not set out in one but in two definite sections-which limit the activities of the department. The first, section 4, provides:
The duties and powers of the minister administering the Department of Health, shall extend to and include all matters and questions relating to the promotion or preservation of the health of the people of Canada over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction, and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, particularly the following matters and subjects.
I shall deal with these matters in a moment. Then there is section 7, which the parliament of that day considered necessary:
Nothing in this act or in any regulations made hereunder shall authorize the minister or any officer of the department to exercise any jurisdiction or control over any provincial or municipal board of health or other health authority operating under the laws of any province.
Just a moment ago my good friend from Ontario complained because the Dominion government was not in a position to go into Montreal during the recent epidemic and take charge of the health situation. That argument is absolutely absurd; it was not received by members of the house and it will not be received throughout the country, because everyone knows that at all times the provinces have insisted that they have local control with regard to health as they have with regard to education and other matters.
It is rather surprising to find hon. gentlemen opposite belittling the efforts which are being made by health authorities and by those who have charge of the health of this country; listening to hon. gentlemen opposite tonight the impression might go abroad that no health measures are being carried out in Canada. That is not true; it is well known to be untrue. In each province we have live health organizations under the control of the provincial governments in addition to the municipal health organizations, and generally speaking our municipal health organizations are not inferior to those in other cities on this continent or anywhere in the world. In health matters the city of Toronto is probably as well equipped as any similar city anywhere in the world. It is true there was an outbreak of typhoid in Montreal a year or two ago, due to an infected milk supply and also to the fact that the laboratories were improperly equipped and insufficiently staffed, but now conditions are different. The hon. member for Muskoka indicated that nothing was being 7S594-179
done in Canada and especially in Quebec, but he did not tell this committee that to-day in health matters Quebec is leading all the provinces of Canada.

Cooperation with the provincial, territorial, and other health authorities with a view to the coordination of the efforts proposed or made for preserving and improving the public health, the conservation of child life and the promotion of child welfare;

Carbon monoxide poisoning has been discussed but there is no authority in the Dominion council, any more than there is in this parliament, to say to the people of Canada, " This is what we will do for carbon monoxide poisoning or this is what we will do for typhoid."

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The province of Alberta enacted legislation at the last session.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is quite
true, but my hon. friend cannot claim for a moment that this committee, composed as it was and with an agenda of this kind, did not produce some good after three days of discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The trouble is that we cannot see it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: My hon. friend seemed to think that the establishment and maintenance of a national laboratory for public health and research work should be the whole thing; that the Health department should be an incident to that section and not that section an incident to the Health department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is the way the hon. member has talked.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It is the biggest thing in the department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The establishment of that laboratory for public health and research woi'k is an important thing, but the department is doing other work which is not being done elsewhere in Canada. These various services were within other departments and we have established research laboratories and testing laboratories to deal with all questions relating to our food products. The best of chemists procurable have been employed and the work being done is equal to that being carried out in any laboratory of like character in the world.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The Excise department
used to do that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
They did, but we do not think that they did it as well as we are doing it at the present time. We have very excellent men in Doctor Harris and Mr. Lancaster. They are recognized authorities on this subject and if anyone would take the time to go through these laboratories and see the class of work which is being done in re-

speechtext:
My hon. friend
speaks of the United States with some apparent appreciation of their greatness; does he know that it is only within the last few years that that great country has established a laboratory of health research.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Doctor Wiley has been doing the food work for over fifteen years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
He has been doing it for years and doing it very effectively. Previous to the establishment of a health laboratory in Canada very little of that work had been done.
I will have something further to say before the discussion in regard to public health and research work closes. It would seem to my hon. friend that the establishment of a laboratory such as he speaks of requires only the expenditure of money. Money is about the least requirement for a laboratory of that character; personnel is the main and important one.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The government has not got it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
During the last one hundred years there have been only a few men with the talent for research who have made great discoveries. It is hard to say just where we could get the research men to go into a laboratory of that kind; we certainly would not get them by putting applications through the Civil Service Commission asking for men to apply for positions in a research laboratory. In the development of the laboratory work which is now being done we hope to train the men who will do the research work of the future.
The government is not opposed in any way to a laboratory for health research, and it is well known to parliament and to Canada that the government is giving considerable thought to research along other lines. Buildings are being constructed and it is hoped that we will soon have our own laboratories and our own personnel for the research work of the Health department, and I believe that some day we will be able to , create a laboratory and do the work which my hon. friend is desirous that we should rush into at once.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The minister must be careful and not duplicate the work which is being done in the Connaught laboratories, for instance, and other places of that kind.

Mr. KING' (Kootenay):	This class of
research work has not been done, as a rule, by governments. The work of Pasteur and of other great scientists has been carried on under very unfavourable conditions. Work of that character is being done in laboratories such as those, of the Rockefeller institute and of our universities. Men are continually in training and the faculty knows the men who have the proper qualifications for research work and they endeavour to retain those men. It is well known that the Rockefeller institute-does not go to the universities with a view to.>
taking that class of men away, because they know that such a procedure is resented.. Where they find a man with those qualifications they arrange with the university authorities to relieve him of some of his other duties which he may be doing within the university.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
